newsitem.title: GERMANY: Former spymaster faces German justice again.
newsitem.headline: Former spymaster faces German justice again.

text.p: Legendary East German spymaster Markus Wolf went on trial on Tuesday charged with three cases of Cold War skulduggery which could have come straight from the pages of a classic espionage thriller.
The suave 73-year old, who ran East Berlin's foreign intelligence network for over 30 years, strongly rebutted prosecutors' charges in his opening statement to the court.
"I declare myself to be not guilty," said Wolf, dressed in a smart dark double-breasted suit. "I did not violate either the constitution of the country I served or its laws."
The trial is a last bid by prosecutors to bring to book the elusive figure dubbed "the man without a face" as his western counterparts for decades had little idea what he looked like.

Wolf was convicted of treason in the same Duesseldorf courtroom in 1993. But Germany's highest court overturned the decision in 1995 saying Wolf could not be convicted of spying on what was then a foreign country -- West Germany.
This time prosecutors have charged Wolf with crimes under East German law -- abduction, coercion and causing bodily harm.

"Now the Federal Prosecutor is trying to turn me into an ordinary criminal," Wolf told the court, accusing prosecutors of staging the trial for purely political reasons to discredit the East German system and its leaders.
Prosecutors also revived a charge from Wolf's original trial of acting as a secret agent for a foreign power. The charges relate to intelligence work in the 1950s and 1960s.
Wolf said he was not directly involved in the 1962 kidnapping of a former officer from the Ministry for State Security (Stasi) who had fled to Austria.
Prosecutors say the officer, Walter Thraene, and his girlfriend were abducted, beaten unconscious and spirited back to East Germany, where they served lengthy prison terms.

Wolf ran a network of around 4,000 foreign-based agents from his East Berlin headquarters. One of his biggest coups was planting "mole" Guenter Guillaume inside Chancellor Willy Brandt's office -- leading to Brandt's resignation in 1974.
In his statement to the court, Wolf also defended his record in the case of Georg Angerer, an East German citizen held in custody for half a year in 1959.

Prosecutors say intelligence officials tried to force Angerer to make defamatory statements about Brandt, who was then mayor of West Berlin. Angerer had known Brandt when they were in exile in Norway in the 1930s.
But Wolf insisted Angerer was held not to help fabricate lies about Brandt but to find out whether the Social Democrat politician had ever collaborated with the Nazis.
"It was not about constructing something false about Willy Brandt," Wolf told the court. "It was about proving something."

The third case prosecutors have brought against Wolf involves a 1955 attempt by East German intelligence to persuade Christa Trapp, a German translator at the U.S. High Commission in West Berlin, to spy for them.
"I have to say that the Christa Trapp case has left no trace in my memory," Wolf told the small high-security courtroom packed with German and international reporters.

The prosecution alleges Trapp and her mother were forced into East Berlin, separated and detained overnight. "When (Trapp) refused to cooperate, she was told she would never see her mother again," prosecutor Wolfgang Siegmund said.

Wolf said even though he could not recall the case, it appeared to be the kind of attempt to recruit an agent which was the common practice of intelligence services for capitalist and communist countries at the time.
